question_text: Which publication gives routeing measures adopted by the IMO?
What is the principal purpose of an ocean passages publication?
option_d: To provide planning guidance on routes, currents, climate and hazards

question_text: When selecting an ocean route, the vessel's seasonal load-line zone affects primarily the:
Why are prevailing currents considered during passage planning?
option_a: They can affect course made good, speed and fuel consumption

After drawing a great-circle track on a gnomonic chart, how is it normally transferred to a Mercator chart?
option_a: As a series of waypoints joined by rhumb-line legs
option_d: By converting it to magnetic bearings

question_text: On a Mercator chart, a rhumb line appears as:
option_a: A straight line crossing meridians at a constant angle
option_b: A curve convex to the equator

question_text: The chief advantage of a great-circle route between distant points is that it:
option_c: Usually gives the shortest surface distance

question_text: A composite great-circle route is commonly chosen to:
The vertex of a great circle is the point at which the track reaches its:
For a same-name difference of longitude in rhumb-line sailing, the east-west component is found using:
A vessel steams 360 miles at 15 knots. Ignoring delays, the passage time is:
A ship has 420 miles remaining and makes good 14 knots. Its approximate time to go is:
When clocks are advanced one hour for daylight-saving time, local civil time becomes:
option_a: One hour ahead of standard time

question_text: When converting an ETA from UTC to a zone whose description is minus 8, zone time is:
The most important early consideration when planning a landfall is to:
option_a: Ignore tidal streams until visual contact
option_c: Choose a conspicuous, positively identifiable approach with safe water

question_text: When making a landfall after a long ocean passage, the navigator should initially assume that:
option_d: The lighthouse will be visible at charted range

question_text: A vessel joining a traffic lane should normally do so:
option_a: At as small an angle to the traffic flow as practicable

question_text: A vessel crossing a traffic separation scheme should cross:
option_a: On a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the traffic flow

question_text: The main objective of ship routeing is to:
option_c: Improve safety in converging or congested areas and environmentally sensitive waters

question_text: In a mandatory ship-reporting system, the master should:
option_b: Comply with the prescribed report content and timing
option_c: Transmit cargo details on open VHF regardless of instructions
option_d: Wait for the pilot to report

question_text: Before entering a VTS area, the bridge team should first confirm:
option_d: Reporting points, channels, required information and local procedures

question_text: VTS information received by a vessel:
option_b: Must always be followed as a helm order
option_d: Supports decision-making but does not replace the master's responsibility

question_text: When navigating near ice, the safest general practice is to:
option_a: Maintain maximum speed to reduce exposure
option_b: Proceed at a safe speed with enhanced lookout and engines ready

question_text: The master should obtain ice information before entering an ice region because:
option_a: Load lines do not apply in ice
option_b: Ice has no effect on radar
option_d: Ice conditions can change rapidly and may invalidate the planned route

question_text: When ice accretion is expected on deck, the principal stability concern is:
option_b: A rise in KG and possible asymmetric heeling moment

question_text: Prior to sailing, the bridge team should verify that:
option_a: The passage plan is appraised, completed, checked and approved by the master
option_b: Only the first course is plotted
option_c: The ECDIS safety contour is left at its previous value
option_d: The pilot will prepare the plan

question_text: Before arrival in port, a bridge checklist should include:
option_b: Steering tests, communications, navigation equipment and berthing information
option_c: Cargo claims from the last port

question_text: Approaching high traffic density, the master should consider:
option_a: Reducing the lookout to avoid distraction
option_b: Strengthening the bridge team and ensuring engines are ready as appropriate

question_text: In reduced visibility, the bridge team should:
option_a: Post a proper lookout, use radar systematically and proceed at a safe speed
option_c: Maintain sea speed until another vessel is sighted

question_text: A watch handover should be postponed when:
option_a: The relieving officer is fully informed
option_b: The ship is in open water
option_c: The master is on the bridge
option_d: A manoeuvre or hazardous situation demands the officer's full attention

question_text: During watch handover, the relieving officer should be informed of:
option_b: Position, course, traffic, weather, equipment status and standing orders

question_text: The daily at-sea bridge routine should include checking:
option_d: Chronometers, compass errors, chart corrections and navigation equipment as applicable

question_text: During master-pilot exchange, which item is essential?
option_d: The intended passage, manoeuvring data, tug use, berthing plan and local hazards

question_text: After a pilot boards, responsibility for safe navigation:
option_c: Remains with the master and bridge team

question_text: Near an offshore installation, a vessel should confirm:
option_b: That AIS may be switched off
option_c: Safety-zone restrictions, fairways, traffic and any reporting requirements
option_d: That the installation must alter course

question_text: A safety zone around an offshore installation is intended primarily to:
option_d: Reduce collision risk and protect the installation and vessels

question_text: The most suitable position-fixing method in confined coastal waters is normally:
option_b: Frequent fixes using independent, well-spread observations

question_text: The interval between position fixes should be reduced when:
option_b: The vessel enters confined water or approaches danger
option_d: The vessel is stopped in safe anchorage

question_text: Which factor most strongly determines the maximum safe fixing interval?
option_b: Distance and time to the nearest navigational hazard

question_text: For a three-bearing visual fix, accuracy is generally improved when the bearings:
option_a: Are converted to magnetic after plotting
option_c: Are all of the same object
option_d: Are well spread and taken nearly simultaneously

question_text: A transit bearing is especially valuable because it can provide:
option_b: A sensitive indication of cross-track movement

question_text: Parallel indexing is primarily used to:
option_c: Continuously monitor a vessel's track relative to radar-conspicuous features

question_text: A parallel index line should be prepared with reference to:
option_d: A suitable fixed radar target and the planned passing distance

question_text: The principal precaution when using parallel indexing is to:
option_c: Assume radar range has no error
option_d: Treat it as monitoring information and continue independent position fixing

question_text: For celestial observations, the best selection of stars generally has:
option_a: Similar azimuths and very low altitudes

question_text: A star at an extremely low altitude is usually avoided because:
In the intercept method, an observation giving Ho greater than Hc is plotted:
option_b: At right angles to the meridian only

question_text: In the intercept method, an observation giving Ho less than Hc is plotted:
option_c: At the DR position without an intercept

question_text: The intercept distance in nautical miles equals:
option_a: The difference between Ho and Hc in minutes of arc
option_c: The difference in longitude in degrees

question_text: A celestial position line is drawn:
option_b: Parallel to the equator in all cases
option_d: Perpendicular to the body's azimuth through the intercept point

question_text: When advancing an earlier celestial position line, it is moved by the:
option_b: Course and distance made good to the common time

question_text: A long-period celestial running fix is especially sensitive to errors in:
option_b: Course and distance made good between sights

question_text: A systematic error in several position lines tends to:
option_b: Displace the lines in a consistent manner

question_text: The most probable position from several celestial lines should account for:
option_c: Geometry, observation quality and any identified systematic error

question_text: A small cocked hat does not by itself prove an accurate fix because:
option_b: A common systematic error may shift all position lines
option_d: Three lines cannot form a fix

question_text: Random observational errors are reduced most effectively by:
option_a: Using one object repeatedly at the same instant

question_text: A position fix should be treated as unreliable when:
option_c: Independent methods disagree beyond their expected errors

question_text: When GNSS and visual positions differ materially, the officer should first:
option_d: Investigate datum, sensor, plotting and identification errors and obtain another independent fix

question_text: A continuous position-monitoring system should be checked against:
option_a: Independent fixing methods and the passage plan

question_text: An official electronic chart used in ECDIS is:
option_b: An ENC issued by or on the authority of a hydrographic office

question_text: When ECDIS is operating in RCDS mode, the navigator should remember that:
option_a: Raster charts lack the full object intelligence and alarms of ENCs
option_b: All chart objects can be queried
option_c: Safety contours are generated automatically from vector data
option_d: No paper-chart backup is ever required

question_text: An ECDIS safety contour should be selected after considering:
option_b: Draught, squat, heel, tide, UKC policy and uncertainty

question_text: If the exact desired safety contour is unavailable in an ENC, ECDIS normally uses:
Over-reliance on ECDIS can be reduced by:
option_b: Cross-checking with radar, visual, echo-sounder and other independent information

question_text: A compilation-scale warning indicates that:
option_a: The chart is being displayed at a scale larger than its compilation scale
option_b: The vessel is outside GNSS coverage

question_text: Before accepting an ECDIS route, the officer should:
option_a: Run route checks and visually inspect every leg at suitable scale
option_c: Assume alarms prove the route safe

question_text: A GNSS position may be precise but unsafe to use if:
option_b: The wrong chart datum or sensor offset is applied

question_text: AIS information should not be used as the sole means of collision avoidance because:
option_c: It may be incorrect, delayed, absent or based on entered data

question_text: A speed log supplying speed through the water is most directly useful for:
option_c: Assessing vessel motion relative to the water and some collision calculations

question_text: A Doppler log in bottom-track mode measures speed relative to:
The echo sounder reading should be interpreted after allowing for:
option_b: Transducer setting, draught, tide and seabed characteristics

question_text: Gyro error determined from a transit is found by comparing:
option_c: Observed gyro bearing with the charted true bearing

question_text: If true bearing is 120 degrees and gyro bearing is 117 degrees, the gyro error is:
If true bearing is 080 degrees and gyro bearing is 084 degrees, the gyro error is:
Magnetic compass deviation is obtained after allowing the observed compass bearing for:
option_c: Variation to relate magnetic and true directions

question_text: If variation is 5 degrees west and magnetic bearing is 090 degrees, the true bearing is:
Compass error from a celestial body is determined by comparing its:
option_a: Calculated true azimuth with observed compass bearing

question_text: A rendezvous calculation requires both vessels' positions, courses and speeds primarily to determine:
When calculating a SAR rendezvous, the intercept point must be:
option_b: At the midpoint regardless of speed
option_d: Reachable by both vessels at the same time

question_text: The On-Scene Coordinator's central function is to:
option_b: Assume legal command of every ship
option_c: Suspend reports to the rescue coordination centre
option_d: Coordinate search units and communications in accordance with the SAR plan

question_text: On taking OSC duties, an officer should establish:
option_d: A common search plan, communications schedule and reporting arrangement

question_text: Search patterns should be selected mainly according to:
option_c: Datum uncertainty, target type, available units, weather and visibility

question_text: The principles of a safe navigational watch require the OOW to:
option_a: Maintain situational awareness and remain in charge until properly relieved
option_b: Leave the bridge whenever alarms are active
option_c: Rely on the helmsman for collision assessment
option_d: Perform distracting administrative work in traffic

question_text: The composition of the bridge team should be increased when:
option_a: Workload, traffic, weather or navigational complexity rises
option_d: Only one radar is available in open ocean

question_text: Fatigue risk in bridge-team planning is best controlled by:
option_d: Adequate rest, realistic schedules, task allocation and calling additional personnel

question_text: Standing orders should clearly state:
option_d: When the master must be called and the master's expectations for the watch

question_text: Night orders should:
option_a: Supplement standing orders with voyage-specific instructions and call points
option_d: Remove the OOW's duty to act

question_text: If circumstances require immediate action, the OOW should:
option_a: Take necessary action and call the master without delay
option_b: Wait for the master before acting

question_text: Engineering-watch readiness during pilotage should reflect:
option_a: The need for prompt propulsion response and the passage risk assessment

question_text: A systematic radar plot primarily provides:
option_a: The exact intentions of the target
option_d: Target relative motion, CPA, TCPA and an assessment of collision risk

question_text: A target with constant bearing and decreasing range indicates:
option_c: The target will pass safely astern

question_text: Before acting on an ARPA vector, the OOW should confirm:
option_b: Tracking is stable and vector mode, length and sensor inputs are understood
option_c: AIS and ARPA speeds are identical

question_text: A relative vector on a relative-motion display represents:
option_a: The target's motion relative to own ship

question_text: A true vector is most useful for assessing:
option_a: The target's estimated true course and speed

question_text: After own ship alters course, ARPA solutions may be temporarily unreliable because:
option_d: The system needs time to stabilise new motion estimates

question_text: When several targets present collision risk, action should be planned to:
option_a: Make a succession of small alterations
option_b: Maximise CPA with only the closest target
option_c: Produce safe passing distances for the developing situation as a whole

option_a: Understanding sensor dependencies and cross-checking independent sources
option_b: Accepting the integrated display without verification
option_c: Using AIS as the primary position sensor
option_d: Selecting identical alarm limits in all waters

question_text: A rate-of-turn indicator is particularly useful when:
option_c: Monitoring and controlling a planned alteration in confined water

question_text: An anemometer assists command decisions by indicating:
option_a: Relative or true wind information, subject to system configuration

question_text: Blind pilotage should be prepared using:
option_c: A detailed plan with radar references, parallel indexes, clearing limits and team roles
option_d: Visual bearings that cannot be seen

question_text: During blind pilotage, position should be monitored by:
option_b: Multiple appropriate means with clearly assigned bridge-team tasks

question_text: The principal limitation of an electronic navigational aid is that:
option_b: It can fail or present plausible but erroneous information

question_text: If a primary position sensor fails during coastal navigation, the immediate response should include:
option_a: Continuing unchanged until the next port
option_c: Changing to verified alternatives and increasing manual position monitoring

question_text: ECDIS route monitoring does not remove the need to:
option_c: Maintain lookout and verify position by appropriate independent means

question_text: A chart permit or update failure should prompt the officer to:
option_b: Identify the affected coverage and provide an approved, corrected alternative before sailing
option_d: Ignore the warning if GNSS works

question_text: A tropical revolving storm's dangerous semicircle is generally the side where:
option_c: Storm translational wind adds to rotational wind

question_text: The first priority when avoiding a tropical revolving storm is to:
option_a: Determine the vessel's position relative to the storm and keep well clear using forecast and observed data

question_text: A rapid fall in barometric pressure with increasing swell may indicate:
option_b: Approach of a severe weather system

question_text: An advantage of commercial weather routeing is:
option_a: Access to forecasts and route optimisation support

question_text: A disadvantage of weather routeing advice is that:
option_a: It is prohibited on ocean passages
option_d: Forecast uncertainty and vessel-specific limitations still require onboard judgment

question_text: At a standard port, tidal height at an intermediate time is found from:
option_a: The port's predicted high and low waters using the appropriate interpolation method

question_text: For a secondary port, high- and low-water predictions are normally obtained by:
option_a: Adding chart datum to air draught
option_b: Using the standard port values unchanged
option_c: Applying published time and height corrections to the standard port

question_text: Neap tides generally have:
option_c: A smaller tidal range than springs

question_text: Under-keel clearance at a given time is based on available depth minus:
option_d: The vessel's effective draught, including relevant allowances

question_text: Available water depth is normally calculated as:
option_a: Charted depth minus height of tide
option_d: Charted depth plus height of tide

question_text: A charted drying height of 1.5 m means the feature is:
option_d: Measured from mean sea level only

question_text: For overhead clearance, the relevant water-level calculation compares:
option_c: The obstruction's charted vertical clearance with the vessel's air draught and tide reference

question_text: If masthead-to-keel distance is 42 m and draught is 10 m, the static air draught is:
A channel has charted depth 9 m and height of tide 2.5 m. For a draught of 10 m, static UKC is:
A bridge has vertical clearance 35 m at the stated datum. If the effective air draught is 33 m, the clearance margin is:
Tidal stream atlases normally express stream rates relative to:
option_d: A stated number of hours before or after high water at a reference port

question_text: To estimate tidal stream at an intermediate time, the navigator should:
option_a: Use wind direction as the stream
option_b: Use the relevant tidal stream table or atlas and interpolate where instructed
option_c: Assume the spring rate at all times

question_text: Following engine failure in confined water, the bridge should immediately:
option_b: Wait for shore instructions before acting
option_c: Assess danger, warn traffic and relevant authorities, display signals and use anchors/tugs as appropriate

question_text: After steering-gear failure, the first bridge actions include:
option_c: Engaging emergency steering procedures, reducing risk and establishing communications

question_text: If radar fails in restricted visibility, the master should consider:
option_b: Maintaining full speed because AIS remains
option_c: Continuing without informing the engine room
option_d: Reducing speed, strengthening lookout, using alternatives and moving clear of danger

question_text: On the onset of adverse weather, the bridge should:
option_c: Reassess route, speed, stability, securing and machinery readiness

question_text: When working with a helicopter, the ship should:
option_c: Follow the agreed communications and course/speed instructions and prepare the operating area
option_d: Direct exhaust toward the operating area

question_text: Personnel near a helicopter winching area should:
option_b: Touch the wire before it is earthed if required
option_c: Control loose objects and follow the helicopter crew's instructions
option_d: Stand directly beneath an approaching load

question_text: When recovering survivors from a small craft, the bridge team should consider:
option_d: Lee creation, relative motion, propeller danger and communications

question_text: A navigational standing order requiring the master to be called:
option_a: Transfers the watch to the master automatically
option_b: Does not prevent the OOW taking immediate action for safety
option_c: Permits the OOW to delay collision action

question_text: An adequate engineering watch for arrival should be arranged:
option_b: Early enough to meet manoeuvring and emergency-readiness requirements

question_text: Current Merchant Shipping Notices relevant to navigation should be consulted because they:
option_b: May contain mandatory requirements or detailed implementation guidance

question_text: Marine Guidance Notes generally provide:
option_c: Guidance and interpretation on maritime safety matters

question_text: Marine Information Notes generally communicate:
option_d: Information of a more temporary or administrative nature

question_text: Under the ISM Code, navigation procedures should be:
option_c: Documented within the safety management system and implemented onboard

question_text: The ISM Code requires identified navigation risks to be managed through:
option_a: Shore control of every helm order
option_b: Safe practices, defined responsibilities, procedures and continuous improvement

question_text: A voyage-optimisation measure supporting decarbonisation is to:
option_a: Plan speed and route to reduce unnecessary fuel while preserving safety margins

question_text: Just-in-time arrival can reduce emissions by:
option_b: Avoiding high-speed steaming followed by waiting at anchor

question_text: When optimising for fuel, the master must give priority to:
option_a: The lowest possible speed in every circumstance
option_d: Safety, legal obligations and the prevailing conditions

question_text: Cross-track limits in a passage plan should be:
option_a: Set for each leg with regard to navigable water, hazards and position accuracy

question_text: A no-go area on a passage plan represents:
option_d: Water the vessel must not enter under the planned conditions

question_text: A wheel-over position should allow for:
option_b: Speed, rate of turn, vessel manoeuvring characteristics and environmental effects

question_text: Squat should be allowed for because it can:
option_d: Increase effective draught and alter trim in shallow or confined water

question_text: A clearing bearing is used to:
option_d: Provide a limit indicating whether the vessel remains clear of a hazard

question_text: When a radar conspicuous object and its AIS symbol do not coincide, the officer should:
option_b: Investigate sensor alignment, target data and association before relying on either
option_c: Assume the AIS position is correct
option_d: Move the radar echo to the AIS symbol

question_text: A bridge-team briefing before a critical passage should establish:
option_c: The plan, hazards, roles, call criteria, contingencies and communications

question_text: The final authority to depart from a passage plan when safety requires rests with:
option_d: The master, with actions and reasons properly managed and recorded
